# skill: status-report

Use when a task ends, to report status in a table

# Report status when a task ends

> **The one rule:** every time a task ends, there must be a status table in the task's central file, and the same table in the reply.
> A task with no status table is not finished.
> **Exception:** read-only playbooks (`research` · `review` · software-development: `investigation`) put the table in the reply only and write no file.

---

## 1 · Where to write

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| General work (**default**) | `.claude/superuser/CONTEXT.md`. Edit only `## ความคืบหน้า` (progress). The heading `## รับงานต่อ` (take over) belongs to `handoff` section 5, so write it by the rules there. Touch no other heading. If the file does not exist yet, create it from [`templates/CONTEXT.md`](../superuser/templates/CONTEXT.md). |
| The project has `docs/BUILD-PLAN.md` | Use the form in section 3 instead. Write in one place, never duplicate in two. |
| Several subagents work at the same time | Subagents only **report back**. Let the team lead write the file alone, or the file breaks. |

The location and rules of every file are in [`team-files`](../superuser/references/team-files.md).

---

## 2 · The `## ความคืบหน้า` table

```markdown
## ความคืบหน้า
| งาน | สถานะ | หลักฐาน | อัปเดต |
|---|---|---|---|
| สรุปยอดขายเดือนนี้ (`docs/sales-oct.xlsx`) | เสร็จ | ยอดรวมตรงใบสั่งซื้อ 212/212 · `reviewer` ตรวจแล้ว | 2026-10-21 14:20 |
| รายงานคู่แข่ง 5 ราย | ทำอยู่ | อ่านแหล่งทางการครบ 3/5 | 2026-10-21 14:20 |
| ใบเสนอราคาลูกค้า A | รออนุมัติ | ร่างพร้อมใน `out/quote-A.pdf` · ส่งแล้วย้อนไม่ได้ | 2026-10-21 14:20 |
| ค่าส่งต่างประเทศ | ค้างอยู่ | รอผู้ใช้ยืนยันเรทของขนส่ง | 2026-10-21 14:20 |
| ค้นหาสินค้า (โค้ด) | เสร็จ | test 48/48 · `reviewer` ตรวจแล้ว | 2026-10-21 14:20 |
```

The `## รับงานต่อ` heading that sits below it is written by `handoff` section 5 (one format, used both at the end of a task and at hand-over).

- Status uses the same 5 words as `superuser`: `เสร็จ` (done) · `ทำอยู่` (in progress) · `ติด` (blocked) · `รออนุมัติ` (awaiting approval) · `ค้างอยู่` (pending; not started yet also uses `ค้างอยู่`).
- **Evidence is always required** when you write `เสร็จ`: a number that was really checked · how many items were compared · the file name that was opened · the result from `reviewer`. If it was not checked, write `ยังไม่ได้ตรวจ` (not yet checked). Never write that it passed.
- The checker must not be the same one that did the work. If there is a subagent, name its role in the evidence column.
- The table holds only open tasks, at most 15 rows. A finished task moves to 1 line in `HISTORY.md`. Overwrite the whole heading, never append.
- **ค้างอยู่** (pending) is what the agent cannot continue by itself, because a person must answer or decide. Write it as a question that can be answered, and say whom to ask. If there is none, write `ไม่มี` (none).
- **รออนุมัติ** (awaiting approval) is work that is prepared but irreversible (superuser section 6). Give the command or file that is ready to use. If there is none, leave it out.
- **ข้อเสนอ** (proposals, in the reply) are improvements outside the scope, at most 3. Say what is gained and how much effort it takes. If there are none, leave it out.

---

## 3 · The form for a project that has `docs/BUILD-PLAN.md`

Write `## สถานะล่าสุด` (latest status; overwrite) and `## ประวัติสถานะ` (status history; add a line at the top) in that file instead of `CONTEXT.md`. The heading order, columns, allowed values and row ceiling are in [`build-plan-rules`](references/build-plan-rules.md). **Open it before every write.**

---

## 4 · In the reply

Show "ภาพรวม" (overview, if any) + a table of only **the rows that changed this round** + "ค้างอยู่" + "รออนุมัติ" (if any) + "ข้อเสนอ" (if any) + "ถัดไป" (next), then say where the full table lives (`CONTEXT.md` or `docs/BUILD-PLAN.md`). Do not paste the whole file.

---

## 5 · Checklist before saying it is finished

- [ ] Read the central file from disk before editing (someone else may have edited it)
- [ ] The progress table is overwritten, not appended, and has a date and time
- [ ] Every row that says `เสร็จ` or `ผ่าน` (pass) has evidence · the checker is not the doer
- [ ] You did not set `Approved` yourself
- [ ] `## รับงานต่อ` is updated per `handoff` section 5
- [ ] You touched no other heading in the file
- [ ] BUILD-PLAN form: the numbers in "ภาพรวม" match the table · 1 line is added to `## ประวัติสถานะ` · "ทีมตอนนี้" (current team) has no leftover `ทำอยู่` row for a task that has finished
- [ ] BUILD-PLAN form: run the checker until it passes (the checker is in plugin `superuser`): `python <superuser folder>/skills/polished-document-style/scripts/check_outline.py assets/build-plan-status.md <path of docs/BUILD-PLAN.md>`. It catches missing headings, swapped headings, missing bold cells, changed table headers and cells not yet filled. Other headings in the file (the task table, `## ตัดสินใจเอง`) the checker lets pass.
---

## 6 · What not to do

- Do not create a new status file (`STATUS.md` `progress.md`), because status then scatters across places.
- Do not hide failing items in prose, because a reader of the table will think everything passed.
- Do not append to the table every round, and do not let a subagent write the central file.

---

## Project plan and weekly report

The template for a project plan (timeline · milestone · risk register · Responsible-Accountable-Consulted-Informed (RACI)) and the weekly status report sent to stakeholders is in [`references/project-plan-and-weekly-status.md`](references/project-plan-and-weekly-status.md)

## Link to other skills

| Need | Use together with |
|---|---|
| The task table and the code-writing loop in the same file | `spec-to-code-loop` (plugin `software-development`) |
| A project's document set and document status | `project-doc-set` (plugin `software-development`) |
| Recording context to continue in the next conversation | `handoff` |
| The table of self-made decisions in the same file | `decision-log` |
| Choosing a playbook and finishing every kind of task | `superuser` |

| Names and status of document files | `document-naming` |


## reference: build-plan-rules.md

# Format for projects that have docs/BUILD-PLAN.md

Moved from `SKILL.md` item 3 · open it when the project has `docs/BUILD-PLAN.md`

Write these 2 sections in that file instead of `CONTEXT.md` · no file → create a file holding only the project name, then copy from [`assets/build-plan-status.md`](../assets/build-plan-status.md) (never invent the structure) · **never touch the job table or other sections**
Section order: `## สถานะล่าสุด` (latest status) → job table → `## ประวัติสถานะ` (status history) → `## ตัดสินใจเอง` (decisions made on your own, `decision-log`)

- `## สถานะล่าสุด` — **overwrite the whole section** every time, as the single current picture
- `## ประวัติสถานะ` — **add 1 line at the very top** per job, never delete the old ones, in the format `วันที่ เวลา · งาน · สถานะ · ผล · ทำ <agent> · ตรวจ <agent> · ค้างกี่ข้อ` (date time · job · status · result · made by <agent> · checked by <agent> · how many items pending; if you decided anything on your own that round, append `· ตัดสินใจเอง <count>`)

Section `## สถานะล่าสุด` holds: an update line (date and time · latest job) · **ภาพรวม** (overview: done N/total · in progress · blocked · failed check — counted from the table and must match) · a table `| รายการ | ประเภท | สถานะ | ใครทำ | ใครตรวจ | ผลตรวจ | ค้าง / หมายเหตุ |` (item · type · status · made by · checked by · check result · pending / note) · **ทีมตอนนี้** (team now: 1 row per agent used this round · no subagent, leave it out · starting a new round clears the old rows) · ค้างอยู่ (pending) · รออนุมัติ (awaiting approval) · ถัดไป (next, at most 3) · ข้อเสนอ (proposals)

| Column | Allowed values |
|---|---|
| ประเภท (type) | `เอกสาร` (document) · `ตรวจ` (check) · `ส่งมอบ` (delivery) · `โค้ด` (code) · `build` |
| สถานะ (status), documents | `ยังไม่เริ่ม` (not started) · `Draft` · `Review` · `Approved` · `Archived` (the same set as `polished-document-style`) — `Approved` belongs only to someone who can change it, and an agent may set at most `Review` |
| สถานะ (status), others | the 5 words in `SKILL.md` item 2 |
| ผลตรวจ (check result) | `ผ่าน — <evidence>` · `ไม่ผ่าน — <what failed>` · `ยังไม่ได้ตรวจ` · `—` |

The table holds every item of the project, not just this round's work (items not touched copy their old values), at most 25 rows
Code work (a full example table · type `build`/`ส่งมอบ` · mobile app evidence) → the extension in plugin `software-development` → `superuser` → `references/code-extensions.md`


## reference: project-plan-and-weekly-status.md

# Project plan and weekly status — stakeholder templates

Template for the agent `project-manager` · moved from the agent file (2026-10-14) · the short status table at the end of a job is in the SKILL.md of `status-report`, while this file holds the project plan and the weekly report for stakeholders

**สารบัญ:**

- [Standard Output: Polished Project Plan](#standard-output-polished-project-plan)
- [Standard Output: Polished Status Report](#standard-output-polished-status-report)

## Standard Output: Polished Project Plan

```markdown
# Project Plan: <Project Name>

| | |
|--|--|
| **Project Lead** | @pm-name |
| **Sponsor** | @sponsor |
| **Status** | ทำอยู่ (วางแผน) |
| **Start Date** | YYYY-MM-DD |
| **Target End** | YYYY-MM-DD |
| **Budget** | ฿XX,XXX |

---

## Objective

> One-sentence goal that fits in a tweet.

## Scope

| In Scope | Out of Scope |
|-------------|-----------------|
| ... | ... |

## Timeline

![ผังเวลาโครงการ: Discovery → Build → Launch](figures/fig-01.png)

**รูปที่ 1 —** ผังเวลาโครงการ วาดด้วย `diagram-figures` (plugin `software-development` · house style) แล้วฝังเป็นไฟล์ภาพ · ไม่ใช้ Mermaid ในแผนที่ส่งผู้เกี่ยวข้อง

## Milestones

| # | Milestone | Target Date | Owner | Status |
|:-:|-----------|:-----------:|:------|:------:|
| 1 | Requirements approved | YYYY-MM-DD | @ba | ค้างอยู่ |
| 2 | Architecture signed off | YYYY-MM-DD | @architect | ค้างอยู่ |
| 3 | Minimum Viable Product (MVP) feature complete | YYYY-MM-DD | @dev-lead | ค้างอยู่ |
| 4 | User Acceptance Testing (UAT) passed | YYYY-MM-DD | @qa | ค้างอยู่ |
| 5 | Production launch | YYYY-MM-DD | @devops | ค้างอยู่ |

## Risk Register

| ID | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Score | Mitigation | Owner |
|:--:|------|:----------:|:------:|:-----:|------------|:------|
| R-001 | Payment vendor delay | Medium | High | 6 | Plan B vendor | @architect |
| R-002 | Resource availability | Low | Medium | 2 | Cross-training | @pm |

> **Score = Likelihood × Impact** (1-9 scale)

## Dependencies

| Type | Dependency | Owner | Status |
|------|------------|:------|:------:|
| External | Payment gateway (Application Programming Interface, API) | Vendor X | ติด |
| Internal | Design team availability | @design-lead | ทำอยู่ |
| Technical | New cloud account | @devops | ทำอยู่ |

## Responsible-Accountable-Consulted-Informed (RACI) Matrix

| Activity | PM | BA | Arch | Dev | QA | DevOps |
|----------|:--:|:--:|:----:|:---:|:--:|:------:|
| Requirements | A | R | C | I | C | I |
| Architecture | A | C | R | C | I | C |
| Implementation | A | I | C | R | C | C |
| Testing | A | I | I | C | R | I |
| Deployment | A | I | C | C | I | R |
```

| | |
|--|--|

## Status by Track

| Track | Status | Notes |

# skill: database-design

Use when designing or changing a database schema

# Database design

> **One rule:** the schema is the hardest thing in a system to change.

## When to use this skill

- Designing the database of a new system or a new module
- Adding or changing a table, column, relationship or index
- Writing a migration, especially once the system holds real data
- A query is slow and you suspect the schema or an index

Not for: overall architecture → `architecture-patterns` · endpoints and JSON shapes → `api-conventions` · passwords, tokens, permissions → `auth-implementation-patterns` · running migrations in a pipeline → `cicd-and-release`

**Syntax specific to each database, data types compared, and the migration commands of each Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) tool** are in `references/per-stack.md`.

---

## 1 · Choose the database type first

| Criterion | Relational (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL) | Document (MongoDB) |
|---|---|---|
| Data has clear relationships and needs joins | ✓ | ✗ must be done by hand |
| Data shape is uncertain and differs per record | Careful: use a JSON column | ✓ |
| Needs transactions across several tables | ✓ | Careful: possible but costlier |
| Reports, totals, analysis | ✓ | ✗ |
| Very heavy writes, log/telemetry | Careful | ✓ or use a time-series database |

> **The default is relational.** Choose document only when you **can answer why**.
> "More flexible" is not a reason. It means the design is not done yet.

**You can mix them**: use relational as the base, and store data of uncertain shape in a `jsonb` column.
In almost every case this is better than running 2 separate databases.

---

## 2 · Naming rules — choose once, use across the whole system

| What you name | Format | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Table | `snake_case` **plural** | `orders`, `order_items` |
| Column | `snake_case` singular | `created_at`, `total_amount` |
| primary key | `id` | `id` |
| foreign key | `<singular table>_id` | `customer_id` |
| Join table | `<a>_<b>` in alphabetical order | `role_users` ✓ (not `user_roles`) |
| index | `ix_<table>_<column>` | `ix_orders_customer_id` |
| unique | `ux_<table>_<column>` | `ux_users_email` |
| foreign key constraint | `fk_<table>_<target table>` | `fk_orders_customers` |
| check constraint | `ck_<table>_<topic>` | `ck_orders_total_non_negative` |

**Do not:**

- Wrong: put the data type in the name, such as `name_varchar`, `is_active_bit`
- Wrong: prefix a column with the table name, such as `order_order_date` (it is already in the `orders` table)
- Wrong: use reserved words such as `user`, `order`, `group`, `key`, which need quotes every time. Use `users`, `orders` instead.
- Wrong: use abbreviations people cannot read, such as `cst_nm`. It saves 8 characters but costs 3 years of confusion.

> SQL Server may use `PascalCase` if the existing project already does.
> **Using one style across the whole system matters more than which style is right.** Do not switch midway.

---

## 3 · Columns every table must have

```sql
id           bigint / uuid   PRIMARY KEY
created_at   timestamptz     NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
updated_at   timestamptz     NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
```

Add these as needed:

| Column | Add when | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `deleted_at timestamptz` | Data must be recoverable, or the law requires keeping it | **Every query must filter on it**, or deleted data shows up |
| `created_by` / `updated_by` | You must be able to say who changed it | Store the user id, not the name |
| `row_version` / `xmin` | Several people can edit at the same time | Use with the ETag in `api-conventions` |
| `tenant_id` | Multi-tenant system | See section 10 |

> **soft delete (delete by only setting a flag) has a cost**: every unique constraint must be rethought.
> `ux_users_email` will block signing up with the same email again, even though the old account was deleted.
> Fix it with a partial index: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`

---

## 4 · Choose the identifier type

| Type | Pros | Cons | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bigint` auto-increment | Small, fast, index does not fragment, easy to read when tracing problems | Next id can be guessed · ids collide when merging data from several places | Default, single system, single database |
| **UUIDv7 / ULID** | Sorted by time · can be generated on the app side · no collisions | 16 bytes · hard to read by eye | Distributed system · id needed before saving · id appears in a URL |
| `UUIDv4` fully random | No collisions, cannot be guessed | **index fragments, and writes get clearly slower with lots of data** | Avoid if you can |

> **UUIDv4 as a primary key is the most common trap.**
> Fully random values make every insert land in the middle of the index structure.
> You do not feel it at tens of thousands of rows, but at tens of millions it gets so slow you must rebuild.
> If you must use a UUID, use **v7**, which starts with the time, so it grows in order like bigint.

**A number people see is not the primary key**: a purchase order number such as `SO-2026-00042` that the customer refers to
should be stored as a separate column with a unique constraint, and the primary key should not be shown.

---

## 5 · How much normalisation is enough

**Always start at Third Normal Form (3NF)**: each fact is stored in one place.

You may denormalise (accept duplicated data) only when all 3 of these hold:

1. You measured and it is truly slow (with numbers, not a feeling).
2. You know how the duplicated data will be updated so that the copies match.
3. You wrote the reason in the table comment.

**A commonly accepted exception**: data that must be "frozen" at a point in time.
The product price in a purchase order must be copied into `order_items.unit_price`
and not joined to `products.price`, because today's price is not the price on the day the customer bought.

---

## 6 · Four data types people get wrong all the time

Details of the 4 data types people get wrong all the time (money · time · enum or status · boolean), with examples, are in [`data-types`](references/data-types.md).

## 7 · index — where to put one so it works

**Must have:**

- Every foreign key (most databases **do not create it automatically**)
- Columns in the `WHERE` of frequently run queries
- Columns used in `ORDER BY` together with pagination

**composite index (an index on several columns): column order matters**

```sql
-- query: WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_tenant_status_created
  ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);
```

Order the columns by condition type: **equals → range → sort**.
An index `(a, b)` works for a query that filters on `a` alone, but **not** for one that filters on `b` alone.

**Do not add an index when:**

- The table has fewer than a few thousand rows, because the database reads the whole table faster
- The column has many repeated values, such as `is_active` where 95% are true
- The table is written far more often than read, because every index adds cost on every write

> **Measure before guessing**: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (PostgreSQL) or the execution plan (SQL Server)
> tells you whether the index is really used. Guessing that it "should help" is wrong more often than right.

---

## 8 · Constraints live in the database, not only in the app

| Rule | Where it should live |
|---|---|
| Email must not repeat | `UNIQUE` in the database **and** a check in the app so the error message looks nice |
| Amount must not be negative | `CHECK (total_amount >= 0)` |
| A purchase order must have a real customer | `FOREIGN KEY` |
| Status must be one of the defined values | `CHECK` or a lookup table |

> **Reason:** the app is not the only thing that touches the data. There are also urgent data-fix scripts,
> import jobs at 3 a.m., and a 2nd service written later.
> A constraint in the database is the last gate that nobody can skip.

**Choose `ON DELETE` on purpose:**

| Option | Meaning | Use with |
|---|---|---|
| `RESTRICT` (the default you should use) | Cannot delete while children exist | Almost every case |
| `CASCADE` | Delete all the children too | True components, such as `order_items` |
| `SET NULL` | Child becomes parentless | Optional relationships |

If you put `CASCADE` in the wrong place just once, deleting 1 customer wipes 10 years of purchase history with it.

---

## 9 · migration — change the schema without taking the system down

The expand-and-contract steps, and example migrations that deploy without downtime, are in [`migrations`](references/migrations.md).

Data warehouses for analysis (star schema · SCD · ELT) are in [`warehouse-modeling`](references/warehouse-modeling.md) · pipelines that can rerun safely (incremental · backfill · data quality tests · checklist before going to production) are in [`data-pipeline-patterns`](references/data-pipeline-patterns.md).

## 10 · Multi-tenant systems

| Style | How separate | Cost | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| A `tenant_id` column in every table | Low: one slip and data leaks across tenants | Cheapest | Many tenants, small data per tenant |
| A separate schema per tenant | Medium | Migrations must loop over every schema | Tens to hundreds of tenants |
| A separate database per tenant | Highest | Most expensive | Enterprise customers who require separation |

> **Important:** if you choose the `tenant_id` style, **enforce it at the lowest layer, not by adding it to each query**.
> Use the database's row-level security, or the ORM's global filter.
> A single query that forgets `WHERE tenant_id = ?` shows one customer's data to another,
> and no error appears at all.

---

## 11 · Personal data

- Keep a list of **which columns are personal data**. Without this list you cannot answer the question "where is my data?".
- National ID numbers, credit card numbers and health data: encrypt at the column level, or do not store them at all if not needed.
- Set a **retention period** per table, and have a real job that deletes accordingly.
- Data must be deletable when the owner asks, and soft delete alone does not count as deleting.
- Never copy real data onto a developer machine without masking it.

---

## 12 · Anti-patterns

- **One table that stores everything** (`entity` / `attribute` / `value`): every query becomes hard.
- **`varchar(255)` on every column**: this number means nothing. Set it from real data.
- **Several values in one column**, such as `"1,4,7"`: cannot search it, cannot add a constraint. Use a join table.
- **No foreign key because "the app takes care of it"**: one day you will have orphan rows.
- **An index on every column just in case**: writes get slower and storage bloats, with no one benefiting.
- **`SELECT *` in real code**: the code breaks every time a column is added.
- **Business logic in triggers**: problems are untraceable, because nobody sees it running.
- **A migration that also writes data**, mixed with the structure change: on rollback the data is lost.
- **Changing the schema on production by hand**: at the next deploy the schema will not match.


## reference: data-pipeline-patterns.md

# Data pipeline patterns — incremental, backfill, quality, catalog

Every pipeline must give the same result when run again (`principle-safe-to-rerun`) and must always pass values into SQL as parameters.

**สารบัญ:**

- [Pipeline Patterns](#pipeline-patterns)
- [Data Catalog Pattern](#data-catalog-pattern)
- [Production Pipeline Checklist](#production-pipeline-checklist)

## Pipeline Patterns

### Pattern 1: Incremental Loading

```sql
-- dbt incremental model
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='id') }}

SELECT
    id,
    user_id,
    event_type,
    created_at
FROM {{ source('raw', 'events') }}
WHERE 1=1
{% if is_incremental() %}
    -- Only new since last run
    AND created_at > (SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM {{ this }})
{% endif %}
```

### Pattern 2: Late-arriving Data

```sql
-- Don't just look at last 1 hour, look back further for late events
WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'  -- buffer
  AND created_at > (SELECT MAX(created_at) - INTERVAL '1 day' FROM target)
```

### Pattern 3: Data Quality Tests (dbt)

```yaml
# models/marts/orders.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: orders
    description: One row per order
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: customer_id
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('customers')
              field: customer_id
      - name: amount
        tests:
          - dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
              expression: ">= 0"
```

### Pattern 4: Idempotent Backfills

```python
# Backfill should be safe to re-run
async def backfill(start_date: date, end_date: date):
    for d in date_range(start_date, end_date):
        # DELETE then INSERT in one transaction (idempotent); value passed as a parameter, never in the SQL string
        async with db.transaction():
            await db.execute("DELETE FROM target WHERE date = $1", d)
            await load_for_date(d)
```

### Pattern 5: Real-time Pipeline

```python
# Kafka consumer pattern
from kafka import KafkaConsumer

consumer = KafkaConsumer(
    'events',
    bootstrap_servers='kafka:9092',
    enable_auto_commit=False,  # ← manual commit = at-least-once (not exactly-once)
    isolation_level='read_committed',
)

batch = []
for message in consumer:
    batch.append(parse(message))

    if len(batch) >= 1000:
        # Write first, commit the offset after. Kafka and the DB share no
        # transaction, so a crash between the two replays this batch
        # (at-least-once). Make the write idempotent so a replay is harmless.
        with db.transaction():
            db.bulk_upsert('events', batch, key=('topic', 'partition', 'offset'))  # unique key + ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
        consumer.commit()  # only after the DB write succeeds
        batch = []
```

For exactly-once effect: idempotent upsert as above, or store the offsets in the
same DB transaction as the data and seek to them on start (skip `consumer.commit()`).

## Data Catalog Pattern

For every table, document:

```yaml
- table: dim_customer
  description: Slowly-changing customer master
  owner: data-team
  freshness: hourly
  source: postgres.app.users (CDC)
  pii: yes
  retention: 7 years
  columns:
    - name: customer_key
      description: Surrogate key
    - name: customer_id
      description: Natural key from source system
    - name: email
      pii: yes
```

## Production Pipeline Checklist

- [ ] Schema validation at ingestion
- [ ] Schema evolution handled (additive only)
- [ ] Tests on critical columns (uniqueness, not-null, ranges)
- [ ] Monitoring on row counts, freshness, error rates
- [ ] Alerting (PagerDuty / Slack) on failures
- [ ] Backfill procedure documented + tested
- [ ] Idempotency verified
- [ ] Lineage visible (dbt docs, OpenLineage)
- [ ] PII tagged
- [ ] Access controls per dataset
- [ ] Cost monitored (query / storage)


## reference: data-types.md

# 6 · Four data types that are routinely got wrong

### Money

```sql
total_amount   numeric(19,4)   NOT NULL      -- ถูก:
currency       char(3)         NOT NULL      -- ถูก: ISO 4217 เช่น THB
total_amount   float / double                -- ผิด: 0.1 + 0.2 ไม่เท่ากับ 0.3
```

> Wrong: **float for money is a bug you cannot find.** The total drifts by 1 satang per line
> You only learn at month-end close, and cannot trace back where it drifted

### Time

| Store | Use | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Time an event happened | `timestamptz` (SQL Server uses `datetimeoffset`) stored as UTC | Thailand has no daylight saving, but systems sold abroad do |
| Birth date, due date | `date` | no time, no time zone |
| Shop opening hours | `time` + a separate time zone column | |

**Rule:** store UTC and convert to `+07:00` only at display time; never store raw Thai time in a `timestamp` that has no zone

**Buddhist Era (BE)**: always store Common Era (CE), then convert to BE at display time
If you store the year 2569 in the database, every function will compute durations wrongly

### enum / status

| Approach | Good when | Bad when |
|---|---|---|
| Lookup table + foreign key | values can be added without a deploy, has Thai/English names, and has a display order | needs a join |
| `check constraint` as text | constant values that rarely change | adding a value needs a migration |
| PostgreSQL `enum` type | fast, small | **a value cannot be removed** and the order cannot be changed |
| raw `int` | — | ✗ reading `status = 3`, nobody knows what it means |

### boolean

- Name it as a positive statement: `is_active` (right) · `is_not_disabled` (wrong)
- **If a third state might appear in the future, do not use boolean**, because `is_approved` will become `approval_status`
  within 6 months, once "รออนุมัติ" (awaiting approval) is added

## reference: migrations.md

# 9 · migration — change the schema without taking the system down

**3 rules:**

1. **Forward only**: a migration that has been merged must not be edited; if it is wrong, write a new one over it
2. **1 migration does one thing**: easy to trace problems, and rollback is exact
3. **Old-version code and the new-version schema must work together**, because during a deploy both versions of the code always run at the same time

### expand / contract — the standard steps for a change that destroys something existing

Example: rename the column `name` → `full_name`

| Deploy round | Database | Code |
|:--:|---|---|
| **1 · Expand** | add `full_name` (nullable) | write to both columns · read from `name` |
| **2 · Migrate** | copy old data in batches | read from `full_name`, fall back to `name` if it has no value |
| **3 · Contract** | set `NOT NULL` · drop `name` | read and write only `full_name` |

3 rounds looks slow, but every round can roll back without losing data
If you do it in one round, you must accept that the system has to go down

**Commands that lock the table until the system hangs** (be extra careful on large tables):

- Adding a column with both `DEFAULT` and `NOT NULL` at once — newer PostgreSQL does this fast, and MySQL 8.0.12 and up can add a column as INSTANT (changing a data type still rewrites the table)
- Changing a data type
- Creating a plain index; use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` instead (PostgreSQL) or `ONLINE = ON` (SQL Server)

**Always test a migration against a copy of real data**, because a migration that runs in 0.2 seconds on your own machine
may take 40 minutes on production and hold the table lock the whole time

## reference: per-stack.md

# Syntax and tools per database and ORM

**Contents:** 1 Data types compared · 2 PostgreSQL · 3 SQL Server · 4 MySQL / MariaDB · 5 MongoDB · 6 Entity Framework Core (.NET) · 7 Prisma / Drizzle (Node) · 8 Alembic (Python) · 9 Slow query commands

1. [Data types compared](#1--data-types-compared)
2. [PostgreSQL](#2--postgresql)
3. [SQL Server](#3--sql-server)
4. [MySQL / MariaDB](#4--mysql--mariadb)
5. [MongoDB](#5--mongodb)
6. [Entity Framework Core (.NET)](#6--entity-framework-core-net)
7. [Prisma / Drizzle (Node)](#7--prisma--drizzle-node)
8. [Alembic (Python)](#8--alembic-python)
9. [Slow query commands](#9--slow-query-commands)

---

## 1 · Data types compared

| To store | PostgreSQL | SQL Server | MySQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Auto-increment id | `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` | `bigint IDENTITY(1,1)` | `BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT` |
| UUID | `uuid` | `uniqueidentifier` | `BINARY(16)` or `CHAR(36)` |
| Money | `numeric(19,4)` | `decimal(19,4)` | `DECIMAL(19,4)` |
| Time + time zone | `timestamptz` | `datetimeoffset(3)` | `TIMESTAMP` (store UTC) |
| Date only | `date` | `date` | `DATE` |
| Unlimited-length text | `text` | `nvarchar(max)` | `TEXT` / `LONGTEXT` |
| Thai text | `text` (already UTF-8) | **`nvarchar` only** | `utf8mb4` |
| True/false | `boolean` | `bit` | `TINYINT(1)` |
| JSON | `jsonb` (can be indexed) | `nvarchar(max)` + `JSON_VALUE` | `JSON` |
| Binary file | `bytea` (or store outside the database) | `varbinary(max)` | `BLOB` |

> **SQL Server + Thai**: `varchar` turns Thai characters into `?`.
> Use `nvarchar` and always write literals as `N'ข้อความ'`.
>
> **MySQL must use `utf8mb4`**, because MySQL's character set named plain `utf8`
> stores only 3 bytes per character, so emoji and some other characters are lost.

---

## 2 · PostgreSQL

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  order_no      varchar(20)  NOT NULL,
  customer_id   bigint       NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  status        varchar(20)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft',
  total_amount  numeric(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  currency      char(3)      NOT NULL DEFAULT 'THB',
  meta          jsonb,
  created_at    timestamptz  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at    timestamptz  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at    timestamptz,
  CONSTRAINT ck_orders_total_non_negative CHECK (total_amount >= 0),
  CONSTRAINT ck_orders_status CHECK (status IN ('draft','confirmed','shipped','cancelled'))
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_orders_order_no ON orders (order_no) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at DESC);
```

**Create an index without locking the table:**

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_orders_status ON orders (status);
-- Must not run inside a transaction · if it fails it leaves an index in invalid state: DROP it and redo
```

**Update `updated_at` automatically:**

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN NEW.updated_at = now(); RETURN NEW; END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_orders_touch BEFORE UPDATE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();
```

**Row-level security for multi-tenant systems:**

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint);
-- The app sets this per connection: SET app.tenant_id = '42';
```

**Common PostgreSQL traps** (ideas from wshobson postgresql-table-design · version numbers are the version where the behaviour began)

| Trap | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| `timestamp` (no time zone) silently drops the offset, so a `+07:00` machine and UTC store values with different meanings | Always `timestamptz` |
| `serial` creates a separate sequence whose permissions and `DROP` do not follow the table | `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` (PG 10+) |
| `ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL` on a big table risks a long lock | With a constant `DEFAULT` the table is no longer rewritten (PG 11+) · a function DEFAULT such as `now()` still rewrites the whole table |
| `ADD CONSTRAINT` (FK · CHECK) scans the whole table while holding the lock | Use `... NOT VALID` first, then run `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` as a separate statement (lighter lock) |
| DDL queues behind a long transaction, and every query after it waits too | Run `SET lock_timeout = '5s'` before every DDL, and rerun if it times out |
| A unique index lets `NULL` repeat on many rows | `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG 15+) or a partial index `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` |
| `LIKE '%คำ%'` and `ILIKE` do not use a btree index | Extension `pg_trgm` + GIN index · for serious text search use `tsvector` |
| `jsonb` search with `->>` does not use an index | GIN index on the column (`@>` · `?`) or an expression index on `(meta->>'key')` |
| `count(*)` over the whole table to show a page count | Use the estimate from `pg_class.reltuples`, or drop the total count (cursor pagination) |

---

## 3 · SQL Server

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id            bigint IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
  order_no      nvarchar(20)   NOT NULL,
  customer_id   bigint         NOT NULL,
  status        nvarchar(20)   NOT NULL CONSTRAINT df_orders_status DEFAULT N'draft',
  total_amount  decimal(19,4)  NOT NULL CONSTRAINT df_orders_total DEFAULT 0,
  created_at    datetimeoffset(3) NOT NULL CONSTRAINT df_orders_created DEFAULT sysdatetimeoffset(),
  updated_at    datetimeoffset(3) NOT NULL CONSTRAINT df_orders_updated DEFAULT sysdatetimeoffset(),
  row_version   rowversion,
  CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customers FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id),
  CONSTRAINT ck_orders_total_non_negative CHECK (total_amount >= 0)
);

CREATE INDEX ix_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at DESC)
  WITH (ONLINE = ON);   -- Enterprise / Azure SQL only
```

- `rowversion` works directly as an ETag to detect conflicting edits.
- To sort Thai correctly, set the collation `Thai_100_CI_AS` at the column or database level.
- The old `datetime` has a precision of only 3.33 milliseconds. Use `datetime2` / `datetimeoffset` instead.

---

## 4 · MySQL / MariaDB

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  order_no     VARCHAR(20)   NOT NULL,
  customer_id  BIGINT        NOT NULL,
  total_amount DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at   TIMESTAMP     NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at   TIMESTAMP     NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  UNIQUE KEY ux_orders_order_no (order_no),
  KEY ix_orders_customer_id (customer_id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customers FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4 COLLATE=utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
```

- From MySQL 8.0.12, `ADD COLUMN` can use `ALGORITHM=INSTANT` (before 8.0.29 it could add only at the end of the table). Changing a data type still rewrites the table (dev.mysql.com online DDL, checked 22 Oct 2026 (B.E. 2569)). For big tables that need a rebuild, use `pt-online-schema-change` or `gh-ost`.
- Set the server time to UTC (`default_time_zone = '+00:00'`).

---

## 5 · MongoDB

```js
db.createCollection("orders", {
  validator: { $jsonSchema: {
    bsonType: "object",
    required: ["orderNo", "customerId", "totalAmount", "createdAt"],
    properties: {
      orderNo:     { bsonType: "string" },
      customerId:  { bsonType: "objectId" },
      totalAmount: { bsonType: "decimal" },   // wrong: do not use double for money
      createdAt:   { bsonType: "date" }
    }
  }}
});
db.orders.createIndex({ orderNo: 1 }, { unique: true });
db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 });
```

- Embed when the child data is **always read together with the parent and does not grow without limit**. Otherwise use references.
- One document has a 16 MB ceiling, so an array that keeps growing will hit it one day.
- Use `Decimal128` for money, and nothing else.

---

## 6 · Entity Framework Core (.NET)

```bash
dotnet ef migrations add AddOrderStatus
dotnet ef migrations script <from> <to> -o migrate.sql   # right: review the SQL before the real run
dotnet ef database update                                # dev only
```

> **On production, run the reviewed script, not `database update`.**
> That command needs the app's connection to have permission to change the schema, which it should not have in the first place.

```csharp
modelBuilder.Entity<Order>(e => {
    e.ToTable("orders");
    e.Property(x => x.TotalAmount).HasColumnType("decimal(19,4)");
    e.HasIndex(x => new { x.Status, x.CreatedAt }).HasDatabaseName("ix_orders_status_created");
    e.HasQueryFilter(x => x.DeletedAt == null);          // soft delete across the whole system
    e.Property(x => x.RowVersion).IsRowVersion();        // detect conflicting edits
});
```

---

## 7 · Prisma / Drizzle (Node)

```prisma
model Order {
  id          BigInt   @id @default(autoincrement())
  orderNo     String   @unique @map("order_no") @db.VarChar(20)
  totalAmount Decimal  @map("total_amount") @db.Decimal(19, 4)
  status      String   @db.VarChar(20)
  createdAt   DateTime @default(now()) @map("created_at") @db.Timestamptz(3)
  customer    Customer @relation(fields: [customerId], references: [id])
  customerId  BigInt   @map("customer_id")

  @@index([status, createdAt], name: "ix_orders_status_created")
  @@map("orders")
}
```

```bash
npx prisma migrate dev --name add_order_status   # dev — creates the migration file
npx prisma migrate deploy                        # production — runs only the existing ones
```

- Prisma's `Decimal` returns an object, not a number. Calculate with `decimal.js` and do not convert to float.
- `BigInt` cannot be converted to JSON directly. Convert it to a string at the API layer.

---

## 8 · Alembic (Python)

```bash
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add order status"
alembic upgrade head
alembic downgrade -1
```

Split into 3 migrations (1 migration does one thing):

```python
# 1) schema: add a nullable column
def upgrade():
    op.add_column("orders", sa.Column("status", sa.String(20), nullable=True))

# 2) data: backfill existing values (on a big table, do it in small batches)
def upgrade():
    op.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'draft' WHERE status IS NULL")

# 3) schema: enforce NOT NULL and create the index
def upgrade():
    op.alter_column("orders", "status", nullable=False)
    # CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY must not run inside a transaction, so step out of Alembic's transaction
    with op.get_context().autocommit_block():
        op.create_index("ix_orders_status_created", "orders", ["status", "created_at"],
                        postgresql_concurrently=True)
```

> `--autogenerate` **does not see** renames (it reads them as a drop plus a new add, so the data is lost).
> Always read the file it generates before you commit.

---

## 9 · Slow query commands

| Database | Command |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) <query>;` · extension `pg_stat_statements` |
| SQL Server | Turn on "Include Actual Execution Plan" · `sys.dm_exec_query_stats` |
| MySQL | `EXPLAIN ANALYZE <query>;` · `performance_schema` |
| MongoDB | `db.orders.find(...).explain("executionStats")` |

**Danger signs to fix:** `Seq Scan` / `Table Scan` on a big table ·
estimated row count differs from the actual by more than 10 times · a `Nested Loop` that runs hundreds of thousands of times


## reference: warehouse-modeling.md

# Warehouse modeling — ELT, stack, star schema, SCD

For an analytics warehouse, not an application database.

**สารบัญ:**

- [ELT vs ETL (Modern Default: ELT)](#elt-vs-etl-modern-default-elt)
- [Tech Stack (2026 Recommendations)](#tech-stack-2026-recommendations)
- [Schema Design: Star/Snowflake](#schema-design-starsnowflake)
- [SCD (Slowly Changing Dimensions)](#scd-slowly-changing-dimensions)

## ELT vs ETL (Modern Default: ELT)

```
ETL (old way):
Source → Transform → Warehouse
        ↑
        Limited compute, slow

ELT (modern):
Source → Load raw → Transform in warehouse
                    ↑
                    Snowflake/BigQuery scale
```

> **2026 default: ELT with dbt** — load raw to warehouse, transform with SQL via dbt

## Tech Stack (2026 Recommendations)

> The tool list comes from model knowledge and has not been checked against official websites (รอยืนยัน, awaiting confirmation). Check before recommending.

### Warehouse / Lake
| Tool | Best for | Cost |
|------|----------|------|
| **Snowflake** | Pure warehouse, separation of compute/storage | $$|
| **BigQuery** | Serverless, ad-hoc, GCP shops | $$|
| **Databricks** | Unified lake + warehouse, ML-heavy | $$$|
| **DuckDB** | Local dev, embedded analytics | $free |
| **Redshift** | AWS-native, legacy | $$|
| **Postgres** | Small data (<1TB), simplicity | $|

### Transformation
- **dbt** — SQL-based, version controlled, tested (industry default)
- **SQLMesh** — newer alternative to dbt, stronger features

### Orchestration
- **Airflow** — most popular, mature
- **Prefect** — modern Python-native
- **Dagster** — software-engineering approach to pipelines

### Stream Processing
- **Kafka + Flink** — high throughput, exactly-once
- **Kinesis Streams + Flink** — AWS-native
- **Pub/Sub + Dataflow** — GCP-native
- **Materialized views** (Snowflake, BigQuery) — for simple cases

### Ingestion
- **Airbyte** — open source, many connectors
- **Fivetran** — managed, expensive but reliable
- **Estuary** — modern, streaming-first
- **Custom** — for sources not covered

## Schema Design: Star/Snowflake

```sql
-- Fact table (events / measurements)
CREATE TABLE fact_orders (
    order_key BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_key BIGINT,
    product_key BIGINT,
    date_key INT,
    quantity INT,
    amount NUMERIC(19,4)
    -- foreign keys to dimensions
);

-- Dimension tables (descriptive context)
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
    customer_key BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id VARCHAR,        -- natural key
    name VARCHAR,
    email VARCHAR,
    country VARCHAR,
    -- SCD Type 2 tracking:
    valid_from DATE,
    valid_to DATE,
    is_current BOOLEAN
);
```

> **Star = denormalized, query-fast**
> **Snowflake = normalized dims, save storage**
> **Wide tables / OBT (One Big Table) = even faster for analytics**

## SCD (Slowly Changing Dimensions)

### Type 1: Overwrite
```
Customer Bob lived in Bangkok. Moved to Phuket.
→ Update row, lose Bangkok history
```

### Type 2: New row per change (most common)
```
| customer_key | id | name | city    | valid_from | valid_to   | is_current |
| 1            | 42 | Bob  | Bangkok | 2024-01-01 | 2025-06-30 | false      |
| 2            | 42 | Bob  | Phuket  | 2025-07-01 | 9999-12-31 | true       |
```

### Type 3: Add column
```
Customer table: current_city, previous_city
→ Only most recent change preserved
```

# skill: api-conventions

Use when adding API endpoints or checking API consistency

# Application Programming Interface (API) conventions

> **The one rule:** decide once, apply to every endpoint.
> An API where every endpoint behaves the same, even if "not quite right in theory", is easier to use
> than an API where each endpoint is correct in its own way, because with the latter the caller must guess again every time.

## When to use this skill

- Starting to design the first API of a project
- Adding an endpoint to an existing API and wanting it to match what is there
- Reviewing an API and feeling that its parts are not alike
- Needing to answer "if we change it this way, will clients break?"

Not for: designing all the endpoints of one feature → command `/api-design` · health check, error envelope, graceful shutdown → `web-service-essentials` · tables and relations → `database-design`

**A template of the conventions document that you can copy and use** → `assets/API-CONVENTIONS.md`

---

## 1 · The conventions document must exist

Put the file `docs/API-CONVENTIONS.md` in place (the template is at `assets/API-CONVENTIONS.md`).
Write every decision made from this page into that file, with the date and a short reason.

---

## 2 · Naming URLs

```
GET    /v1/orders                 list
POST   /v1/orders                 create
GET    /v1/orders/{id}            single item
PATCH  /v1/orders/{id}            partial update
PUT    /v1/orders/{id}            replace the whole item
DELETE /v1/orders/{id}            delete
GET    /v1/orders/{id}/items      child resource
POST   /v1/orders/{id}/cancel     an action that is not CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete)
```

| Rule | ✓ | ✗ |
|---|---|---|
| Plural nouns | `/orders` | `/getOrders`, `/order` |
| Lowercase, hyphens | `/purchase-orders` | `/purchaseOrders`, `/purchase_orders` |
| At most 2 levels deep | `/orders/{id}/items` | `/customers/{a}/orders/{b}/items/{c}/logs` |
| Use a verb only when it is truly not CRUD | `POST /orders/{id}/cancel` | `POST /orders/cancelOrder` |

**An action that is not CRUD** (approve, cancel, resend) uses `POST /{resource}/{id}/{action}`.
Do not bend it into a `PATCH` that edits `status`, because a status change usually has more side effects than an ordinary field edit.

**How to use `PATCH`:** pick one style for the whole system. Sending only the changed fields (`merge patch`) is recommended,
and you must define clearly whether `null` means "clear the value" or "leave it alone" (see section 6).

---

## 3 · Versioning

| Method | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **In the path** `/v1/orders` | Obvious, easy to test, easy to cache | The URL changes when the version goes up |
| In a header `Accept: application/vnd.acme.v1+json` | The URL stays fixed | Invisible when debugging, often forgotten |

> **Choose the path** unless there is a specific reason — everyone can see the version from a single line in the log.

**Which changes break callers:**

| Change | Breaks? |
|---|:--:|
| Add a new endpoint | No |
| Add an **optional** field to a request | No |
| Add a field to a response | No* |
| Add a new enum value | **Breaks** — a client whose `switch` covers every value will meet an unknown one |
| Remove/rename a field | **Breaks** |
| Change a data type (`"12"` → `12`) | **Breaks** |
| Make a formerly optional field required | **Breaks** |
| Change the HTTP status returned in an existing case | **Breaks** |
| Make a validation rule stricter | **Breaks** |

\* Only when callers were told from the start to "skip fields you do not recognize".
This must be written in `API-CONVENTIONS.md`, not left to hope.

**Raise the major version only when truly needed**, because every version still open is another body of code to maintain.

---

## 4 · Pagination

**Every endpoint that returns a list must have pagination from day one**, with no exceptions.
A list that "only has a few items" will have 10,000 in 2 years.

| Method | Use when | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| **cursor** `?limit=50&cursor=eyJ...` | Default · lots of data · data is added while the user is browsing | Cannot jump to page 7 |
| offset `?limit=50&offset=100` | Page numbers must be clickable · little data | Slower the deeper the page · if a row is inserted while browsing, data repeats or goes missing |

```jsonc
// GET /v1/orders?limit=2 → 200
{
  "data": [ { "id": "1042" }, { "id": "1041" } ],
  "page": {
    "limit": 2,
    "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6MTA0MX0",   // null when there is no more
    "hasMore": true
  }
}
```

- Always wrap the list in `data`, because a bare array leaves no room to add page information later.
- `limit` has a default and a **ceiling enforced on the server** (for example default 20, maximum 100).
- `totalCount` is expensive to count, so make it optional with `?includeTotal=true`. Do not count every time.
- **The cursor must be opaque** (callers must never decode or build one themselves).

---

## 5 · Filtering · sorting · requested fields

```
GET /v1/orders?status=confirmed&createdAt[gte]=2026-01-01&sort=-createdAt&fields=id,orderNo,total
```

| Topic | Convention |
|---|---|
| Filter by equal value | `?status=confirmed` |
| Several values | `?status=confirmed,shipped` |
| Range | `?createdAt[gte]=...&createdAt[lt]=...` |
| Sort | `?sort=-createdAt,orderNo` — `-` means descending |
| Text search | `?q=สมชาย` kept separate from filtering |
| Select fields | `?fields=id,orderNo` |

- **Accept only the fields you have defined.** If any field name is accepted, you get security holes and queries with no index.
- For an unknown parameter, answering `400` is better than skipping it silently. Otherwise a caller who mistypes gets wrong data without knowing.

---

## 6 · Data formats

| Data | Format | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Field names | `camelCase` across the system | `createdAt` |
| Time | RFC 3339 · UTC · ends with `Z` | `"2026-09-25T09:42:13.482Z"` |
| Date only | `YYYY-MM-DD` | `"2026-09-25"` |
| Money | the number as a **string** + a separate currency | `{ "amount": "1250.00", "currency": "THB" }` |
| identifier | **always a string** | `"1042"` not `1042` |
| enum | `SCREAMING_SNAKE` or `lower_snake`, pick one style | `"CONFIRMED"` |
| Duration | seconds as a number, named so the unit is clear | `"timeoutSeconds": 30` |
| Country / currency / language | ISO 3166 · ISO 4217 · BCP 47 | `"TH"` · `"THB"` · `"th-TH"` |

> **A numeric id in JSON is a time bomb** — JavaScript stores integers safely up to 9,007,199,254,740,991.
> A `bigint` above that is silently rounded at `JSON.parse`, and changing it to a string later is a breaking change.
>
> **Money as a float in JSON** — `1250.10` passed through 2 programming languages may become `1250.0999999999999`.

**`null` and "no field" must mean different things:**

- In a response, a field that exists but has no value is sent as `null`, not dropped, so callers do not have to check 2 cases.
- In a `PATCH`, sending `{"note": null}` means clear the value, and leaving out the `note` key entirely means leave it alone.

**An empty array is `[]`, not `null`**, so callers can loop over it directly.

---

## 7 · Errors

The error format (RFC 9457 · `requestId` · an `errors` array of `{field, code, message}`) and examples live in one place, `web-service-essentials` section 2. Follow that.
What still needs agreement is the **field-level error**:

- **`code` is for programs, `message` is for people.** Never make callers write conditions against the message text.
- Point to the field location with the full path, including array indexes.
- **Return the errors for all fields at once**, not one at a time, so users do not have to submit 5 times.
- If several languages are supported, choose Thai or English text from `Accept-Language`.

**Pick the status to match:** `400` malformed request · `401` not authenticated · `403` authenticated but not permitted ·
`404` does not exist, or you do not want to reveal that it exists · `409` conflicts with the current state · `422` well-formed but the data fails the rules · `429` too many calls

---

## 8 · Repeat calls without repeat effects, and edit conflicts

### idempotency key (a request code — sending it again does not do the work again)

**Required on every `POST` that has a financial effect or sends something out to the outside world.**

```
POST /v1/payments
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c1e10-...        ← created by the caller, kept for use when retrying
```

- The server stores the key together with the result for at least 24 hours.
- Same key with the same body: return the earlier result and do not repeat the work.
- Same key with a **different** body: answer `422` and do not do new work.
- A network drop while waiting for the answer is normal, not a special case, so callers always retry.

### Edit conflicts (optimistic concurrency)

```
GET   /v1/orders/1042        → 200  ETag: "v7"
PATCH /v1/orders/1042        If-Match: "v7"
                             → 200 normally · 412 if someone edited it first
```

Without this, whoever saves second overwrites the first person's work and nobody knows.

---

## 9 · Rate limit

```
X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 997
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1758790000
Retry-After: 42                ← must always accompany a 429
```

If a `429` has no `Retry-After`, the caller must guess, and most guess "try again at once".

---

## 10 · Retiring an endpoint

1. Announce in advance, and say what to use instead.
2. Send these headers in every response of that endpoint:
   ```
   Deprecation: @1790812800
   Sunset: Wed, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT
   Link: <https://docs.acme.co/v2/orders>; rel="successor-version"
   ```
   `Deprecation` follows the Request for Comments (RFC) 9745 standard (Mar 2025). It must be a date in the form `@<unix seconds>` (this example is 1 Oct 2026 00:00 UTC), not `true`. Checked 22 Oct 2026 (B.E. 2569).
3. **Check the logs for who still calls it**, then contact them directly. Do not wait for them to go quiet on their own.
4. Close it only after the announced date, not before.

A fitting period: for an internal API, 1 release cycle. For an API used by outsiders, at least 6 months.

---

## 11 · Check before releasing a new endpoint

Go through every item against the endpoint you added. Fail one and it is not merged yet.

- [ ] The URL is a plural noun per section 2 · sits under a version per section 3 · has no `GET` that changes data
- [ ] Every list has pagination and a page-size ceiling (section 4) · filter and sort use the same parameter names as existing endpoints (section 5)
- [ ] Dates · ids · money are in the formats of section 6 · the response is not a raw database entity
- [ ] Every error follows `web-service-essentials` §2 and has a fixed `code` (section 7) · a request that creates or pays accepts an idempotency key · an edit accepts `If-Match` (section 8)
- [ ] Auth and rate limit are stated (section 9) · it is in OpenAPI, and the cURL examples in the docs really run
- [ ] There is a contract test or an endpoint-level test with at least 1 success case and 1 error case — check the response against OpenAPI in CI · Pact when the caller is on another team · `oasdiff breaking` on every PR: [`references/contract-testing.md`](references/contract-testing.md)

## 12 · Anti-patterns

- **`200 OK` with `{"success": false}`** — monitors and logs will not see that it failed.
- **Verbs in the URL** — `/createOrder`, `/getOrderById`
- **A list with no pagination** — one day it will return 50,000 rows at once.
- **A different date format on each endpoint** — for example `"25/09/2026"`, where nobody knows whether day or month comes first.
- **Sending a database entity out as is** — every time a column is added, the API changes by accident, and internal data may leak.
- **Mixed field names** such as `created_at` and `updatedAt` in one response.
- **A `GET` that changes data** — a web page prefetcher will fire it by itself with nobody clicking.
- **Error messages that keep changing** with no fixed `code`.
- **No documentation** — an OpenAPI generated from the real code is better than hand-written docs that do not match.


## reference: contract-testing.md

# Contract testing — OpenAPI is the contract, and CI checks that the real thing matches

The document `docs/API-CONVENTIONS.md` states the rules · the OpenAPI file states the shape of each endpoint · contract tests are what keep these 2 from being just documents

## 1 · OpenAPI as the contract

- Generate it from the real code (annotations · decorators · the framework's generator) and commit the resulting file — do not hand-write it separately · when the 2 sides differ, the code side is the truth, and the diff in the file is what the reviewer sees
- Every response has a schema, including errors (`web-service-essentials` §2) · every field has a `format` for dates · ids · money, per §6 of the main SKILL.md

## 2 · Check responses against the spec in CI (provider side)

| Tool | What it does | licence | Note (checked 2026-10-23) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schemathesis | reads OpenAPI, builds requests from the schema, fires them at the real service, and checks that responses match the spec and are not 500 · `schemathesis run <url of openapi.json>` | MIT | really fires, creates and deletes data → point it only at dev or staging · Python |
| Prism (Stoplight) | `prism mock <spec>` lets the frontend work before the backend is done · `prism proxy <spec> <upstream>` checks real traffic against the spec | Apache-2.0 | Node ≥ 18.20 · proxy mode can sit in front of the service in a test environment |
| Dredd | checks an API against API Blueprint / OpenAPI 2 (OpenAPI 3 experimental) | MIT | **no longer maintained** (archived 2024-11-08) — do not start using it |

Our default: Schemathesis in a CI job after the service is up with test data (the reset endpoint from `app-verifier-setup`) · failure = no merge

## 3 · Consumer-driven contract — when the frontend team or callers are separate from the backend

- Pact (pact-foundation · MIT): the caller side writes tests of which request/response pairs it uses → produces a pact file → the provider side runs a check against that file in its own CI · the provider can change parts nobody uses without breaking tests
- Use when: the teams are different, release separately, or there is more than 1 caller (mobile + web + partner) · one team does both sides → item 2 is enough
- Pact files are exchanged through a Pact Broker or committed to the provider's repo — agree on one way in `API-CONVENTIONS.md`

## 4 · Check for breaking changes on every PR

- `oasdiff breaking <old spec> <new spec>` (Apache-2.0 · Go · has a Docker image) reports only changes that break existing callers: removing an endpoint or field · a field becoming required · a type change · an enum value removed
- In CI: old spec = the main branch's · new spec = the PR's · on a breaking change → bump to a new version per §3, or deprecate per §10 of the main SKILL.md — do not turn off the check
- Adding an optional field · adding an endpoint · adding an enum value that callers do not crash on in a switch = not breaking

## Check before handing over

- [ ] OpenAPI is in the repo and generated from code · CI fails if the file does not match the code
- [ ] Schemathesis (or equivalent) runs against a service brought up with test data · `oasdiff breaking` runs on every PR
- [ ] Callers in a separate team → at least 1 pact file per caller, and the provider checks it in CI


---

# skill: fsd-writing

Use when writing or reviewing a Functional Specification Document

# Writing a Functional Specification Document (FSD)

> For Thai text, use the business register (`human-writing` `references/thai-grammar.md` section 4).

> **The one rule:** An FSD is done when a developer can read it and **write code without guessing or asking**.
> Every point that forces a guess becomes rework after delivery.

## When to use this skill

- Writing an FSD or Functional Spec for a feature, a module, or a whole system
- Expanding a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) or Business Requirements Document (BRD) to a level detailed enough to build from
- Reviewing someone else's FSD, where you must say what is missing
- A developer keeps asking the same questions while building. That means the FSD is incomplete.

Not for: requirements a customer signs off → `srs-writing` · user stories for a sprint → `user-story-writer` · endpoints of one feature → command `/api-design` (system-wide agreements → `api-conventions`) · tables and columns → `database-design`

## Read more when

| File | Open when |
|---|---|
| [references/worked-examples.md](references/worked-examples.md) | You are writing the first use case, screen, state table, or business rule of the document. Open the full examples and copy the format. |
| [references/edge-cases.md](references/edge-cases.md) | You are writing the errors and edge cases section, and when you review before sending, to cover every case. |
| [references/fsd-vs-srs.md](references/fsd-vs-srs.md) | You are unsure whether a piece of content belongs in the SRS or the FSD. Open this comparison table. |
| [references/stakeholder-doc-templates.md](references/stakeholder-doc-templates.md) | You are writing an easy-to-read FSD for stakeholders (Mode B, the same 11 sections as item 3), or you need a reviewer-friendly template for a use case, API endpoint, or data model. |
| [references/figures.md](references/figures.md) | You are planning which section needs which figure type. |
| [references/outline-sections.md](references/outline-sections.md) | You must decide which section can be skipped. Open this table. The full copy-and-fill outline is in [assets/fsd-outline.md](assets/fsd-outline.md). |
| [references/related-skills.md](references/related-skills.md) | The task needs another skill alongside this one, such as figures, API agreements, or test cases. Open it to see which one. |

## 0 · Look for an existing template first (every time)

Before you use the outline or templates in this file, check whether the user, customer, or project already has its own:

- **Where to look:** the FSD (Functional Specification Document) template from the client or the TOR (terms of reference) · an earlier FSD of the same system · the screen spec template the dev team uses (look in `docs/`, or ask the user one question)
- **Result:** Found → use it (sections, order, field names, numbering) and say in the reply which file it came from. Not found → use the template in this file as a fallback and say that no earlier template was found.
- **Still required in every template:** the FSD/SRS boundary in item 1 and linking codes to use cases.

## 1 · How an FSD differs from an SRS — the boundary must be clear

These two documents get mixed up most often. The result is an SRS so long the customer does not read it, and an FSD so shallow that developers must ask.
The SRS says what the system **must be able to do**. The FSD says **how** the system does it. A dimension-by-dimension comparison is in [references/fsd-vs-srs.md](references/fsd-vs-srs.md).

> **An FSD must not create new requirements.** When you find something the SRS does not cover, **add it to the open-questions list**, mark it `(รอยืนยัน)` (awaiting confirmation), and keep working on the rest.
> The item must be added to the SRS first. Do not write it quietly into the FSD.
> An item that shows up in the FSD with no source is one the customer will refuse to pay for at acceptance.

## 2 · Working order

1. Read the whole SRS or BRD first, then **list the items that are still unclear**. Ask once, at the start, as multiple choice. Every option has evidence (skill `superuser` item 6). Ask only about items where different readings would change the whole deliverable (options = the possible readings, citing the item in the SRS/BRD). Mark the rest `(รอยืนยัน)` and keep going.
2. Confirm who the document is for: developers only (**Mode A**, the default), or also a customer who reads it to sign off (**Mode B**: the same 11 sections in the same order, only laid out so a reviewer can read them easily; see [references/stakeholder-doc-templates.md](references/stakeholder-doc-templates.md)).
3. Go use case by use case, not screen by screen. Screens come from use cases, not the other way around.
4. Write the business rules separately first, then refer to them from the steps (item 7).
5. Build the traceability matrix as you go, not at the end.
6. **Draw, then collect questions.** While drawing the sequence diagram, cancellation flow, and ERD, you will find matters the stories and SRS do not answer (for example, whether a course deducts a session at booking or at attendance). Note them at the end of the document as questions with a proposed answer marked `(รอยืนยัน)`. Do not choose for the customer.
7. Review by item 11 before sending.

## 3 · Document outline

There are 11 sections, in this order: Introduction · Users and permissions · Process overview · Use cases · Screen requirements · State diagram · Business rules · Data and integrations · Errors and edge cases · Traceability matrix · Revision history.
You may skip only the screen requirements if there is no screen, and the state diagram if there are no states. The full outline is in **[`assets/fsd-outline.md`](assets/fsd-outline.md)**. The table of the question each section answers is in [references/outline-sections.md](references/outline-sections.md).

## 4 · Use cases — one format across the document

Every use case has a header table (comes from · actor · preconditions · result on success · frequency), followed by tables for the main steps, alternatives, and error cases. The full example UC-ORD-010 is in [references/worked-examples.md](references/worked-examples.md).

**Rules for a use case:**

- **One use case = one user goal**, not one screen.
- Every use case needs at least one **alternative** and one **error case**.
  A use case with only the smooth path is a use case that is not finished.
- The "what the system does next" column must not be empty. An empty cell means nobody has worked out how the system responds.
- **Always re-check preconditions on the server.** Hiding a button is not access control.
- Write it as alternating "user does → system responds", not as a paragraph of narrative.

## 5 · Screen requirements

The full example SC-ORD-020 with its field table is in [references/worked-examples.md](references/worked-examples.md).

**Every screen must specify all 6 things:**

| Required | Detail |
|---|---|
| Field table | Type · required or not · validation rule · **the actual error message** · default value |
| Permission per role | Which role can see · edit · only read · not see at all |
| The five screen states | Empty · loading · error · partial · success (see `ui-craft`) |
| Actions and results | Which button goes where · which button opens a confirmation box |
| Display rules | Date format · decimals for money · rounding · time zone |
| Data source | Which endpoint or table this field comes from |

> **"The actual error message" means the words the user will really see**, not "show a warning message".
> If you leave it out, the developer will invent one, and the system will end up with ten different phrasings.
>
> **Display rules must be written down.** A "total" that does not say how it rounds
> is a bug you will find at month-end reconciliation.

## 6 · State diagram — the point FSDs forget most often

Anything with a "status" (an order, a leave request, a work ticket, a document) needs a table with the columns From · To · Who can do it · Condition · Side effects, and **must not have only a picture**. A sample table is in [references/worked-examples.md](references/worked-examples.md).

**Rules:**

- **A transition not in the table is a transition that must be rejected.** Write a clear "not allowed" row.
  What is forbidden is the hardest thing to test if nobody wrote it down.
- Every state needs an exit, except a final state that is meant to end.
- Side effects on other systems (email, stock, accounting) belong in this table, not hidden in the steps.

## 7 · Business rules separate from the steps

Each rule has a code, a name, the rule text, and a source. A sample BR-030 is in [references/worked-examples.md](references/worked-examples.md).

- **Write each rule in one place**, then cite it by code from everywhere it applies. If you copy it into three places, someday you will miss one when you change it.
- Every rule needs a **source**. A rule with no source is a rule the team made up.
- A rule that changes over time (tax rate, fee) must say **where it is stored**:
  in code, in a settings table, or editable by the system administrator.

## 8 · Errors and edge cases to answer in full

The edge-case table is what the test team will use, and it is what most FSDs lack. It runs from no data, rapid repeated clicks, and two people editing at once, to insufficient permission. Go through every row in [references/edge-cases.md](references/edge-cases.md) and answer every row that touches the feature.

## 9 · Codes and traceability

```
UC-<module>-<3-digit number>      use case              UC-ORD-010
SC-<module>-<3-digit number>      screen requirement    SC-ORD-020
BR-<3-digit number>               business rule         BR-030
```

Use the same system as `srs-writing`: **number in steps of 10**, and **never reuse a code that has been issued**.

| SRS | FSD | Screen | test case | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FR-ORD-040 | UC-ORD-010 | SC-ORD-020 | TC-ORD-010..014 | Done |
| FR-ORD-040 | UC-ORD-010 · 010-E1 | SC-ORD-020 | TC-ORD-015 | Done |

- **Every use case must trace back to a requirement in the SRS.** If it cannot, someone added a bonus nobody ordered.
- **Every requirement in the SRS must have at least one use case.** If it has none, it was forgotten.
- Alternatives and error cases need their own test cases. Do not count them with the main path.

## 10 · Figures in the document

The table of which section needs which figure type is in [references/figures.md](references/figures.md). The point to remember: a state diagram goes **with the table, not instead of it**.

Every figure in an FSD document (Mode A and Mode B, in markdown and in the file the customer signs off) uses `diagram-figures` in one house style. Screen sketches use `markdown-visuals`.
Mermaid through `software-diagrams` is only for drafts discussed in chat. Do not put it in a delivered document.
**Every figure in one version uses the same color theme**, per `doc-theme` (see `polished-document-style`).

## 11 · Completeness review before sending

**Completeness**

- [ ] Every requirement in the SRS has at least one use case
- [ ] Every use case has at least one alternative and one error case
- [ ] Every screen has a field table with all 5 columns, and the five states
- [ ] Everything that has a status has a state transition table, including the "not allowed" rows
- [ ] Every relevant row of the edge-case table in item 8 is answered

**Clarity**

- [ ] No phrase such as "as appropriate", "automatically", or "as needed" without saying what it means
- [ ] Every error message is written as real words, not "show a warning message"
- [ ] Every number has a unit and a source
- [ ] Field names, status names, and endpoint names are in English, matching what the real code will use

**Consistency**

- [ ] The same word means the same thing throughout (there is a glossary)
- [ ] State names match across the diagram, the table, and the use cases
- [ ] No new requirement that is missing from the SRS

> **Final test:** Have one developer who was not in the meeting read it.
> Every question they ask is one gap to fill before sending.

If nobody is free to read it, use a fresh agent that gets only the FSD file. Have it answer 8–10 questions that a developer and QA would ask (for example, "what happens on a duplicate booking?" and "which states can be reversed?"). Fix every answer that is wrong or says "I don't know" before sending. For the method and the Thai-specific questions (B.E. years · document number format), see [`../srs-writing/references/reader-test.md`](../srs-writing/references/reader-test.md).

**Once code exists, compare the FSD with the real code.** Do this when you review the FSD after a build or before taking over a fix.

- Go code by code through item 9. Search the code and tests for use case codes and screen names (`rg -n "UC-0[0-9]+" --glob '!**/node_modules/**' | head -50`). A code that appears nowhere in the code or tests is a gap. Answer whether it is not built yet or built under another name.
- Compare the 3 places that differ most often: field table (item 5) ↔ validation code · state transition table (item 6) ↔ the code that changes state (including "not allowed" rows) · error messages (item 8) ↔ strings in the code.
- Record each difference as a table `| spec:line | file:line | who is right |` and let a person decide. During the review, do not change the FSD to match the code, and do not change the code to match the FSD.


## reference: edge-cases.md

# Errors and edge cases to answer in full

The test team uses this table, and most FSDs lack it. Go through every row that touches the feature, then write the answers into section 9 of the document.

| Case | Question to answer |
|---|---|
| No data | What does the empty screen show? Is there a button that points to the next step? |
| Very large data | How many items per page? How are they sorted? Can the user search? |
| Rapid repeated clicks | How do you prevent duplicate work? (See idempotency key in `api-conventions`) |
| Two people edit at once | Who wins? What does the other person see? (See ETag in `api-conventions`) |
| Connection drops midway | Is the entered data lost? Does a retry create a duplicate? |
| Session timeout | Does the user get kicked out at once, or is their input kept? |
| Boundary values | 0 · negative values · today · last day of the month · leap year |
| Unusually long text | Does a 200-character name break the layout? |
| Thai text and special characters | Does sorting work? Does search find it? Do emoji break anything? |
| External system does not respond | How many seconds to wait? How many retries? What does the user see meanwhile? |
| Insufficient permission | Visible but not clickable, or not visible at all? **Choose one clearly.** |


## reference: figures.md

# Figures in an FSD document

This table says which figure type belongs in which FSD section. The drawing tool and the color theme are in `SKILL.md` item 10.

| Section | Figure to include |
|---|---|
| 3 Process overview | Flowchart of the work from start to finish |
| 4 Use cases with several parties | Sequence diagram |
| 5 Screens | Screen sketch with numbers pointing to the field table |
| 6 States | State diagram — **a companion to the table, not a replacement** |
| 8 Data | ER diagram of only the tables this module touches |


## reference: fsd-vs-srs.md

# How an FSD differs from an SRS

This table compares the two documents one dimension at a time. Use it when you must decide whether a piece of content belongs in the SRS or the FSD.

| | SRS | FSD |
|---|---|---|
| Question answered | What the system **must be able to do** | **How** the system does it |
| Main readers | Customer · executives · the person who signs off | developer · tester · ux |
| Level of detail | "The system must let users cancel an order" | Where the button sits · which statuses allow cancelling · who has permission · what confirms it · what message appears when cancelling is impossible · what the system does next |
| Changes | Need approval and affect the contract | Can change inside the team, as long as they still meet the same SRS item |
| Content unit | Requirement (`FR-…`) | Use case (`UC-…`) + screen requirement (`SC-…`) |
| Numbers | Come from the customer | Come from the SRS; never invent new ones |


## reference: outline-sections.md

# FSD sections and when you may skip them

This table sums up the question each FSD section answers. The full outline with fill-in hints is in [`../assets/fsd-outline.md`](../assets/fsd-outline.md).

| # | Section | Question it answers | Skippable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Introduction · scope · references | What does this version cover? Which SRS items does it cite? | No |
| 2 | Users and permissions | Who can do what? | No |
| 3 | Process overview | How does the work flow from start to finish? | No |
| 4 | Individual use cases | How is each task done, step by step? | No |
| 5 | Screen requirements | What is on the screen? What does each field validate? | Skippable if there is no screen |
| 6 | State diagram | Which states can this item move between? | Skippable if there are no states |
| 7 | Business rules | Which rules are enforced? | No |
| 8 | Data and integrations | What data is used? Which systems connect? | No |
| 9 | Errors and edge cases | How can it fail, and what does the user see? | No |
| 10 | Traceability matrix | Which SRS item does this come from, and what tests it? | No |
| 11 | Revision history | Who changed what, and when? | No |
